properties.headline: Red Flag Warning issued October 9 at 10:09PM PDT until October 10 at 9:00PM PDT by NWS Reno NV
properties.description:
* AFFECTED AREA...Fire Weather Zones 274 Southern Mono County, 420
Northern Sierra Front including Carson City, Douglas, Storey,
Southern Washoe, Western Lyon, and Far Southern Lassen Counties,
421 Southern Sierra Front including Alpine, Northern Mono, Southern
Lyon, and Western Mineral Counties, 423 West Humboldt Basin in
Pershing County, and 429 Lahontan Basin including Churchill and
Eastern Mineral Counties.

* TIMING...From 11 AM to 9 PM PDT Saturday.

* WINDS...Southwest winds 15 to 25 mph with gusts 35 to 45 mph.

* RELATIVE HUMIDITY...Minimum Humidity between 14 to 22 percent.

* DURATION...3 to 6 hours.

* IMPACTS...The combination of gusty winds and prolonged dry
conditions, even in areas where humidity may not be as low, can
cause fires to rapidly grow in size and intensity before first
responders can contain them.
properties.instruction:
Avoid outdoor activities that can cause a spark near dry vegetation,
such as yard work, target shooting, or campfires. Follow local fire
restrictions. Check weather.gov/reno for updates and
livingwithfire.info for preparedness tips.

properties.areaDesc: Coastal Del Norte; Northern Coastal Humboldt; Southwestern Humboldt; Coastal Mendocino
properties.headline: Beach Hazards Statement issued October 9 at 10:07PM PDT until October 12 at 5:00PM PDT by NWS Eureka CA
properties.description:
* WHAT...Increased threat of sneaker waves expected.

* WHERE...Coastal Del Norte, Northern Coastal Humboldt,
Southwestern Humboldt and Coastal Mendocino Counties.

* WHEN...From late Saturday night through Monday afternoon. .

* IMPACTS...Large, unexpected waves can sweep across the beach
without warning, sweeping people into the sea from rocks,
jetties, and beaches. These sneaker waves can also move large
objects such as logs, crushing anyone caught underneath.
properties.instruction:
Don't be fooled by an ocean that looks calm.  There can be
30 minutes of small waves before a sneaker wave strikes.  Avoid
rocks and jetties. Avoid steep beaches.  Stay much farther back
from the water and never turn your back on the ocean.

properties.headline: Flash Flood Warning issued October 10 at 12:02AM CDT until October 10 at 3:00AM CDT by NWS Birmingham AL
properties.description:
FFWBMX

The National Weather Service in Birmingham has issued a

* Flash Flood Warning for...
East Central Autauga County in central Alabama...
Southern Elmore County in east central Alabama...
Lee County in east central Alabama...
Eastern Lowndes County in south central Alabama...
Montgomery County in south central Alabama...
Northern Barbour County in southeastern Alabama...
Bullock County in southeastern Alabama...
Macon County in southeastern Alabama...
Northwestern Pike County in southeastern Alabama...
Russell County in southeastern Alabama...

* Until 300 AM CDT.

* At 1202 AM CDT, Doppler radar indicated thunderstorms producing
heavy rain across the warned area. Between 2 and 4 inches of rain
have fallen. Additional rainfall amounts of 2 to 4 inches are
possible in the warned area. Flash flooding is ongoing or expected
to begin shortly.

HAZARD...Flash flooding caused by thunderstorms.

SOURCE...Radar indicated.

IMPACT...Flash flooding of small creeks and streams, urban areas,
highways, streets and underpasses as well as other poor
drainage and low-lying areas.

* Some locations that will experience flash flooding include...
Montgomery, Auburn, Prattville, Phenix City, Opelika, Millbrook,
Tuskegee, Union Springs, Notasulga, Hurtsboro, Midway, Milstead,
Meadville, Smiths, Pike Road, Smiths Station, Coosada, Shorter and
Franklin.

This includes the following highways...
US Highway 431 between mile markers 75 and 145. US Highway 80 near
mile marker 114...and near mile marker 115...and between mile markers
121 and 217. US Highway 82 between mile markers 140 and 178...and
between mile markers 179 and 229. US Highway 231 between mile markers
88 and 96...and between mile markers 97 and 117...and near mile
marker 137. US Highway 280 between mile markers 96 and 106...and
between mile markers 116 and 137. Interstate 65 between mile markers
147 and 180. Interstate 85 between mile markers 1 and 69.
properties.instruction:
Turn around, don't drown when encountering flooded roads. Most flood
deaths occur in vehicles.

properties.areaDesc: Aransas Islands; Kleberg Islands; Nueces Islands; Calhoun Islands
properties.headline: Coastal Flood Advisory issued October 9 at 11:56PM CDT until October 12 at 1:00AM CDT by NWS Corpus Christi TX
properties.description:
* WHAT...For the High Rip Current Risk, dangerous rip currents.
For the Coastal Flood Advisory, minor coastal flooding.

* WHERE...Aransas Islands, Kleberg Islands, Nueces Islands and
Calhoun Islands Counties.

* WHEN...For the High Rip Current Risk, through Sunday morning.
For the Coastal Flood Advisory, until 1 AM CDT Monday.

* IMPACTS...Flooding of lots, parks, and roads with only
isolated road closures expected. Rip currents can sweep even
the most experienced swimmers away from shore into deeper
water. These rip currents can become life-threatening to
anyone entering the surf.
properties.instruction:
If travel is required, allow extra time as some roads may be
closed. Do not drive around barricades or through water of
unknown depth. Take the necessary actions to protect flood-prone
property.

Swim near a lifeguard. If caught in a rip current, relax and
float. Don't swim against the current. If able, swim in a
direction following the shoreline. If unable to escape, face the
shore and call or wave for help.

properties.areaDesc: Buncombe, NC; Henderson, NC
properties.headline: Flood Advisory issued October 10 at 12:13AM EDT until October 12 at 2:00PM EDT by NWS Greenville-Spartanburg SC
properties.description:
...The Flood Advisory continues for the following rivers in North
Carolina...

French Broad River Near at Old Fanning Bridge Rd, 3 W Fletcher
affecting Buncombe and Henderson Counties.

.Heavy rainfall from the remnants of Hurricane Isaias will result in
excessive runoff and significant rises on streams within the upper
French Broad River watershed.  Rainfall will develop overnight
tonight, intensify during the day on Saturday, and maintain intensity
through early Sunday morning before tapering off by Sunday
mid-morning.  Storm-total rainfall of 4-8 inches is expected, with
isolated 8-10 inches possible, across the upper French Broad River
watershed, generally upstream of Etowah.  The highest totals will
occur along the Tanassee and Pisgah ridges, with lesser amounts
within the upper French Broad River valley.  Additionally, 4-6 inches
of rainfall are expected within the Mud Creek watershed in Henderson
County, which is a primary tributary of the French Broad River above
Fletcher.  While there continues to be some uncertainty regarding the
exact location, timing, and amounts of the heaviest rainfall, there
is enough confidence in the current forecast that out-of-bank
conditions are likely for the upper French Broad River.  Therefore, a
River Flood Advisory has been issued for the reach near Fletcher,
with a crest above Action Stage expected around Sunday afternoon.  A
rise above Action Stage will result in nuisance, relatively shallow
flooding of low-lying areas adjacent to the French Broad River,
including farmland, woodlands, low-lying secondary roads, greenways,
parks, and other flood-prone locations.  Additional River Flood
Advisories are possible Saturday, especially for the French Broad
River reach near Blantyre.

More significant rises along the French Broad River are possible, and
those with interests along the river are encouraged to stay weather
aware and up-to-date on the latest stream levels and forecasts at
https://water.noaa.gov/wfo/GSP.  Current reasonable worst-case
scenarios are posted in the ADDITIONAL DETAILS sections below.
Forecast crests above Minor Flood Stage may result in the River Flood
Advisories being upgraded to River Flood Warnings.

* WHAT...Flooding caused by excessive rainfall continues.

* WHERE...French Broad River near at Old Fanning Bridge Rd, 3 W
Fletcher.

* WHEN...Until Monday afternoon.

* IMPACTS...At 10.0 feet, Action/Advisory Stage.  The French Broad
River has exceeded bankfull at the gauge site.  Isolated farmland
flooding is beginning across the French Broad River Valley from
Etowah downstream to Avery Creek upstream of the gauge site.

* At 11.5 feet, Action Stage Flooding continues.  Butler Bridge Rd.
is inundated with up to 6 inches of floodwaters from the French
Broad River, forcing road closure.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...
- At 10:30 PM EDT Friday the stage was 3.6 feet and steady.

properties.areaDesc: Haywood, NC
properties.headline: Flood Advisory issued October 10 at 12:08AM EDT until October 12 at 2:00AM EDT by NWS Greenville-Spartanburg SC
properties.description:
...The National Weather Service in Greenville-Spartanburg has issued
a Flood Advisory for the following rivers in North Carolina...

Pigeon River above Old River Rd (NC 215), 1 SW Canton affecting
Haywood County.

.Heavy rainfall from the remnants of Hurricane Isaias will result in
excessive runoff and significant rises on streams within the upper
Pigeon River watershed.  Rainfall will develop overnight tonight,
intensify during the day on Saturday, and maintain intensity
overnight Saturday before tapering off by early Sunday morning.
Storm-total rainfall of 4-9 inches is expected, with isolated 10-11
inches possible, across the upper Pigeon River watershed, generally
upstream of Canton.  The highest totals will occur along the Pisgah
ridge and in the Shining Rock and Middle Prong Wilderness areas
within the headwaters of the east and west forks of the Pigeon River,
respectively.  While there continues to be some uncertainty regarding
the timing and amounts of the heaviest rainfall, there is enough
confidence in the current forecast that out-of-bank conditions are
likely for the Pigeon River.  Therefore, a River Flood Advisory has
been issued for the reach near Canton, with a crest above Action
Stage expected Sunday morning.  A rise above Action Stage will result
in nuisance, relatively shallow flooding of low-lying areas adjacent
to the Pigeon River, including farmland, woodlands, low-lying
secondary roads, greenways, parks, and other flood-prone locations.

More significant rises along the Pigeon River are possible, and those
with interests along the river are encouraged to stay weather aware
and up-to-date on the latest stream levels and forecasts at
https://water.noaa.gov/wfo/GSP.  Current reasonable worst-case
scenarios are posted in the ADDITIONAL DETAILS sections below.
Forecast crests above Minor Flood Stage may result in the River Flood
Advisories being upgraded to River Flood Warnings.

* WHAT...Flooding caused by excessive rainfall is expected.

* WHERE...Pigeon River at above Old River Rd (NC 215), 1 SW Canton.

* WHEN...From this evening to late Sunday night.

* IMPACTS...At 8.0 feet, Action/Advisory Stage.  Common, nuisance
flooding of low-lying areas adjacent to the Pigeon River is
beginning.  Floodwaters are beginning to impact farmland,
woodlands, nurseries, parks, athletic fields, golf courses,
greenways, and boat-access areas with up to 2 feet of inundation.
Low-water crossings may be inundated with up to 2 feet of
floodwater and become impassable.  Adjacent campgrounds, mobile
home/RV parks, and secondary roads may experience floodwater
inundation of up to 1 foot.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...
- At 11:45 PM EDT Friday the stage was 1.2 feet and steady.
- Forecast...The river is expected to rise to a crest of 8.5 feet
Sunday morning.  A reasonable worst-case crest above Minor Flood
Stage below 11 feet cannot be ruled out.
- Action/Advisory Stage is 8.0 feet.
- Minor Flood Stage is 10.0 feet.

properties.description:
HLSSGX

This product covers EXTREME SOUTHWESTERN CALIFORNIA

**Tropical Storm Rachel Will Bring Coastal Flooding, Wind, and Rain to
Portions of Southern California Sunday**


NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- None

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- A Tropical Storm Watch is in effect for San Diego County
Coastal Areas, San Diego County Deserts, San Diego County
Mountains, and San Diego County Valleys

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 740 miles south-southwest of San Mateo Point CA or about
710 miles south-southwest of Mouth of Tijuana River CA
- 23.8N 123.3W
- Storm Intensity 45 mph
- Movement Northeast or 50 degrees at 9 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

Tropical Storm Rachel is currently just over 700 miles southwest of
San Diego, moving northeast towards Northern Baja. Rachel is expected
to make landfall somewhere near the US/Mexico Border late Saturday
night. Tropical storm level impacts have the potential to impact San
Diego County. A Tropical Storm Watch is in effect for all of San Diego
County. The main concerns with Tropical Storm Rachel are coastal
flooding, wind, and periods of heavy rain. The majority of impacts from
the tropical storm are expected on Sunday.

South swell from Tropical Storm Rachel will arrive on Sunday. The
combination of south and northwest swells, increased onshore winds,
and high tides over 7 feet will maintain a threat of coastal flooding
and beach erosion along beaches in San Diego County. Surf on Sunday is
currently expected to peak at 5 to 8 feet with sets to 9 feet,
decreasing to 3 to 6 feet for Monday and Tuesday. Confidence in
impactful coastal flooding is high, with significant coastal flooding
and beach erosion likely.

Widespread rain is expected on Sunday from Tropical Storm Rachel.
There is expected to be a gradient in rainfall amounts with the higher
amounts on the southeastern side of the storm. We have the highest
confidence that the heaviest rain will occur over San Diego County
mountains and deserts. Peak rainfall rates of 0.50 to 0.60 inches are
possible for the coast and valleys, 0.50 to 0.70 inches per hour
possible for the deserts, and 0.70 to 1 inch per hour for the
mountains. Current forecast has rainfall totals of 0.50 to 1.25 inches
for the coast, valleys, and deserts and 1 to 2.5 inches for the
mountains. Areas of flash and urban flooding are possible, especially
where the maximum rainfall rates occur. The San Diego River at Fashion
Valley is currently forecast to peak at 7.4 feet (just below monitor
stage) Sunday afternoon. Those with interests near the San Diego River
should continue to monitor the forecast.

Increased winds are expected with the onset and passage of Tropical
Storm Rachel. Sustained winds of 39+ mph are expected on the southeast
side of the storm. Based on the current track, more southern and
eastern parts of the county are most likely to see winds of this
magnitude. Regardless, strong sustained winds and wind gusts can be
expected on Sunday. Winds may be enhanced by local terrain with gusts
40 to 55 mph on the desert slopes of the mountains and into the
deserts. Local gusts up to 60 mph possible on mountain ridges.

POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* WIND:
Prepare for hazardous wind having possible limited impacts across
EXTREME SOUTHWESTERN CALIFORNIA. Potential impacts include:
- Damage to porches, awnings, carports, sheds, and unanchored
mobile homes. Unsecured lightweight objects blown about.
- Many large tree limbs broken off. A few trees snapped or
uprooted, but with greater numbers in places where trees are
shallow rooted, especially in coastal and valley locations that
don't typically experience strong winds. Some fences and
roadway signs blown over.
- A few roads impassable from debris, particularly within urban
or heavily wooded places. Hazardous driving conditions on
bridges and other elevated roadways.
- Scattered power and communications outages.

* FLOODING RAIN:
Prepare for life-threatening rainfall flooding having possible
extensive impacts across San Diego County. Potential impacts include:
- Major rainfall flooding may prompt many evacuations and rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may rapidly overflow their banks in
multiple places. Small streams, creeks, canals, arroyos, and
ditches may become dangerous rivers. In mountain areas,
destructive runoff may run quickly down valleys while
increasing susceptibility to rockslides and mudslides. Flood
control systems and barriers may become stressed.
- Flood waters can enter many structures within multiple
communities, some structures becoming uninhabitable or washed
away. Many places where flood waters may cover escape routes.
Streets and parking lots become rivers of moving water with
underpasses submerged. Driving conditions become dangerous.
Many road and bridge closures with some weakened or washed out.

Prepare for dangerous rainfall flooding having possible significant
impacts across San Diego County.

* OTHER COASTAL HAZARDS:
High tides over 7 ft, combined with high surf and gusty onshore winds
will increase the threat for coastal flooding across area beaches.
Additionally surf of 6 to 9 ft will create dangerous swimming
conditions. There is increasing potential for significant coastal
flooding and beach erosion.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials.

* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:
If you live in a place particularly vulnerable to flooding, such as
low-elevation areas near the ocean, in a low-lying or poor drainage
area, or in a valley, plan to move to safe shelter on higher ground.

Now is the time to check your emergency plan and emergency supplies
kit and take necessary actions to protect your family and secure your
home or business.

Always heed the advice of local officials and comply with orders that
are issued.

Closely monitor weather.gov, NOAA Weather Radio and local news
outlets for official storm information. Listen for possible changes
to the forecast.

* ADDITIONAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION:
- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov
- For information on creating an emergency plan see getagameplan.org
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

NEXT UPDATE
-----------

The next local statement will be issued by the National Weather
Service in San Diego CA around 2 AM PDT, or sooner if conditions
warrant.

HLSJAN

This product covers Central Mississippi, Northeast Louisiana, and extreme Southeast Arkansas

HURRICANE ISAIAS HAS MADE LANDFALL ON THE FLORIDA COAST

NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- None

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- A Tropical Storm Warning is in effect for Choctaw, Clarke,
Clay, Forrest, Jasper, Jones, Kemper, Lauderdale, Lowndes,
Neshoba, Newton, Noxubee, Oktibbeha, Webster, and Winston

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 170 miles east of Hattiesburg MS or about 240 miles
east-southeast of Jackson MS
- 30.8N 86.5W
- Storm Intensity 90 mph
- Movement North or 5 degrees at 20 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

Hurricane Isaias has made landfall as a hurricane near Destin
Florida this evening. Though Isaias will gradually weaken as it
moves north across Alabama overnight into Saturday, tropical storm
force wind gusts are possible across portions of East and Northeast
Mississippi.  Gradient wind will increase this evening in
southeastern Mississippi, then stronger gusts are expected overnight
into Saturday across eastern and northeastern Mississippi. Downed
trees and power outages are expected in these areas. Heavy rainfall
and flash flooding are also possible, mainly in the Golden Triangle
area. Threat has trended overall downward. Conditions will improve
late Saturday afternoon into Saturday evening.


POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* WIND:
Protect against hazardous wind having possible limited impacts across
eastern and northeastern Mississippi. Potential impacts in this area
include:
- Damage to porches, awnings, carports, sheds, and unanchored
mobile homes. Unsecured lightweight objects blown about.
- Many large tree limbs broken off. A few trees snapped or
uprooted, but with greater numbers in places where trees are
shallow rooted. Some fences and roadway signs blown over.
- A few roads impassable from debris, particularly within urban
or heavily wooded places. Hazardous driving conditions on
bridges and other elevated roadways.
- Scattered power and communications outages.

Elsewhere across Central Mississippi, Northeast Louisiana, and
extreme Southeast Arkansas, little to no impact is anticipated.

* FLOODING RAIN:
Protect against dangerous rainfall flooding having possible
significant impacts across the Golden Triangle area. Potential
impacts include:
- Moderate rainfall flooding may prompt several evacuations and
rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may quickly become swollen with swifter
currents and overspill their banks in a few places, especially
in usually vulnerable spots. Small streams, creeks, canals, and
ditches overflow.
- Flood waters can enter some structures or weaken foundations.
Several places may experience expanded areas of rapid
inundation at underpasses, low-lying spots, and poor drainage
areas. Some streets and parking lots take on moving water as
storm drains and retention ponds overflow. Driving conditions
become hazardous. Some road and bridge closures.

Protect against locally hazardous rainfall flooding having possible
limited impacts across East Mississippi.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials.


* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:
Now is the time to complete all preparations to protect life and
property in accordance with your emergency plan. Ensure you are in a
safe location before the onset of strong winds or possible flooding.

Closely monitor weather.gov, NOAA Weather radio or local news outlets
for official storm information. Be ready to adapt to possible changes
to the forecast. Ensure you have multiple ways to receive weather
warnings.


* ADDITIONAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION:
- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov
- For information on creating an emergency plan see getagameplan.org
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

NEXT UPDATE
-----------

Service in Jackson MS around 4 AM, or sooner if conditions warrant.

HLSMOB

This product covers portions of southwest Alabama...northwest Florida...south
central Alabama...and inland southeast Mississippi.

**ISAIAS MOVING OVER THE WESTERN FLORIDA PANHANDLE INTO SOUTH CENTRAL ALABAMA**

NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- None

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- A Storm Surge Warning and Hurricane Warning are in effect for
Baldwin Central, Baldwin Coastal, Escambia Coastal, Mobile
Central, Mobile Coastal, Okaloosa Coastal, and Santa Rosa
Coastal
- A Hurricane Warning is in effect for Baldwin Inland, Butler,
Conecuh, Covington, Crenshaw, Escambia, Escambia Inland, Mobile
Inland, Monroe, Okaloosa Inland, and Santa Rosa Inland
- A Tropical Storm Warning is in effect for Choctaw, Clarke,
George, Greene, Perry, Stone, Washington, Wayne, and Wilcox

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 100 miles east of Mobile AL or about 50 miles
east-northeast of Pensacola FL
- 30.8N 86.5W
- Storm Intensity 90 mph
- Movement North or 5 degrees at 20 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

Hurricane Isaias with winds of 90 mph will continue to move north at
near 20 mph into south central Alabama. Significant wind impacts and
life threatening storm surge will remain through late tonight. The
strongest winds will occur near and just to the east of the center,
and storm surge inundation of 5 to 7 feet above normally dry ground
will persist along the coast of the western Florida panhandle.
Potential impacts from these winds include numerous downed trees and
power lines, significant power outages, and some roof damage.

Additional rainfall totals of 2 to 4 inches with localized amounts of
6 inches are possible east of the Alabama River. Areas of flooding are
likely if the higher amounts are realized, with considerable impacts
possible.

POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* WIND:
Protect against life-threatening wind having possible devastating
impacts across the western Florida Panhandle and south central Alabama.
Potential  impacts in this area include:
- Structural damage to sturdy buildings, some with complete roof
and wall failures. Complete destruction of mobile homes. Damage
greatly accentuated by large airborne projectiles. Locations
may be uninhabitable for weeks or months.
- Numerous large trees snapped or uprooted along with fences and
roadway signs blown over.
- Many roads impassable from large debris, and more within urban
or heavily wooded places.
- Widespread power and communications outages.

Also, protect against life-threatening wind having possible limited
to extensive impacts across inland southeast Mississippi and southwest
Alabama.

* SURGE:
Protect against life-threatening surge having possible significant
impacts across the coastal portions of the western Florida panhandle
and Alabama. Potential impacts in this area include:
- Areas of inundation with storm surge flooding accentuated by
waves. Damage to several buildings, mainly near the coast.
- Sections of near-shore escape routes and secondary roads become
weakened or washed out, especially in usually vulnerable low
spots.
- Major beach erosion with heavy surf breaching dunes. Strong and
numerous rip currents.
- Moderate damage to marinas, docks, boardwalks, and piers.
Several small craft broken away from moorings, especially in
unprotected anchorages.

* FLOODING RAIN:
Protect against life-threatening rainfall flooding having possible
extensive impacts across south central Alabama and the western Florida
panhandle. Potential impacts include:
- Major rainfall flooding may prompt many evacuations and rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may rapidly overflow their banks in
multiple places. Small streams, creeks, canals, and ditches may
become dangerous rivers. Flood control systems and barriers may
become stressed.
- Flood waters can enter many structures within multiple
communities, some structures becoming uninhabitable or washed
away. Many places where flood waters may cover escape routes.
Streets and parking lots become rivers of moving water with
underpasses submerged. Driving conditions become dangerous.
Many road and bridge closures with some weakened or washed out.

Protect against dangerous rainfall flooding having possible limited
to significant impacts across interior southeast Mississippi.

* TORNADOES:
Little to no impacts are anticipated at this time across the area.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials.

* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:
It is important to remain calm, informed, and focused during an
emergency. Be patient and helpful with those you encounter.

Rapidly rising flood waters are deadly. If you are in a flood-prone
area, consider moving to higher ground. Never drive through a flooded
roadway. Remember, turn around don't drown!

If in a place that is vulnerable to high wind, such as near large
trees, a manufactured home, upper floors of a high-rise building, or
on a boat, consider moving to a safer shelter before the onset of
strong winds or flooding.

Closely monitor weather.gov, NOAA Weather radio or local news outlets
for official storm information. Be ready to adapt to possible changes
to the forecast. Ensure you have multiple ways to receive weather
warnings.

* ADDITIONAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION:
- For the latest detailed evacuation and shelter information...please
refer to your local emergency management agency at the phone number
or website listed below.
- Coastal Alabama:
- Baldwin County: 251-972-6807 or
www.baldwincountyal.gov/departments/EMA
- Mobile County: 251-460-8000 or mobilecountyema.gov
- Northwest Florida:
- Escambia County: 850-471-6400 or myescambia.com/beready
- Santa Rosa County: 850-983-5360 www.santarosa.fl.gov/emergency
- Okaloosa County: 850-651-7150 or myokaloosa.com/emergency-management
- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

Service in Mobile AL around 4 AM CDT, or sooner if conditions warrant.

properties.areaDesc: Cleveland, NC
properties.headline: Flood Advisory issued October 9 at 11:30PM EDT until October 13 at 2:00AM EDT by NWS Greenville-Spartanburg SC
properties.description:
...The National Weather Service in Greenville-Spartanburg has issued
a Flood Advisory for the following rivers in North Carolina and South
Carolina...

(English) Broad River at Shelby Hwy (SC 18), 4 W Blacksburg
affecting Cleveland and Cherokee Counties.

(English) Broad River above Sandy Run Ck, 3 SSW Boiling Springs
affecting Cleveland County.

.Heavy rainfall from the remnants of Hurricane Isaias will result in
excessive runoff and significant rises on streams within the Broad
River watershed.  Rainfall will develop overnight tonight, intensify
during the day on Saturday, and maintain intensity through early
Sunday morning before tapering off by late Sunday morning.
Storm-total rainfall of 6-8 inches is expected, with isolated 10
inches possible, in the headwaters of the Broad River near Bat Cave,
Chimney Rock, and Lake Lure with significantly lesser amounts
downstream, including near Boiling Springs and Blacksburg, where
storm-total rainfall of 2-3 inches is forecasted.  While there
continues to be some uncertainty regarding the exact location,
timing, and amounts of the heaviest rainfall, there is enough
confidence in the current forecast that out-of-bank conditions are
likely for the Broad River downstream of the heaviest rainfall.
Therefore, River Flood Advisories have been issued, with crests above
Action Stage expected no later than Monday morning.  Rises above
Action Stage will result in nuisance, relatively shallow flooding of
low-lying areas adjacent to the Broad River, including farmland,
woodlands, low-lying secondary roads, greenways, parks, and other
flood-prone locations.

More significant rises along the Broad River are possible, and those
with interests along the Broad River are encouraged to stay weather
aware and up-to-date on the latest stream levels and forecasts at
https://water.noaa.gov/wfo/GSP.  Current reasonable worst-case
scenarios are posted in the ADDITIONAL DETAILS sections below.
Forecast crests above Minor Flood Stage may result in the River Flood
Advisories being upgraded to River Flood Warnings.

* WHAT...Flooding caused by excessive rainfall is expected.

* WHERE...(English) Broad River at above Sandy Run Ck, 3 SSW Boiling
Springs.

* WHEN...From this evening to late Monday night.

* IMPACTS...At 10.0 feet, Action Stage.  The Broad River is beginning
to flood residential yards located off of Abe's Mountain Rd. At
12.0 feet, Minor Flood Stage. Broad River floodwaters may be
approaching the base of residential home foundations between Abe's
Mountain Rd. and the river.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...
- At 10:15 PM EDT Friday the stage was 1.7 feet and steady.
- Forecast...The river is expected to rise to a crest of 11.7 feet
Monday morning.  A crest above the Minor Flood Stage of 12 feet
is possible.  A reasonable worst-case crest near the Moderate
Flood Stage of 14 feet cannot be ruled out.
- Action/Advisory Stage is 10.0 feet.
- Minor Flood Stage is 12.0 feet.
properties.instruction:
If you are in the Advisory area, remain alert to possible flooding or
the possibility of the Advisory being upgraded to a Warning.

For detailed information including observed and forecast stages,
flood impacts, flood history, FEMA Flood Hazard Layers, and more,
please visit: https://water.noaa.gov/wfo/GSP

The next statement should be issued Monday evening before 1130 PM
EDT.

properties.headline: Tropical Cyclone Local Statement issued October 9 at 11:29PM EDT by NWS Peachtree City GA
properties.description:
HLSFFC

This product covers North and Central Georgia

**TROPICAL STORM WARNING IN EFFECT FOR WEST-CENTRAL GEORGIA**

NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- None

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- A Tropical Storm Warning is in effect for Chattahoochee,
Harris, Heard, Macon, Marion, Meriwether, Muscogee, Pike,
Schley, Stewart, Sumter, Talbot, Taylor, Troup, Upson, and
Webster

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 240 miles south-southwest of Atlanta GA or about 140
miles southwest of Columbus GA
- 30.8N 86.5W
- Storm Intensity 90 mph
- Movement North or 5 degrees at 20 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, FL around 9:30 PM EDT.
As of 11 PM EDT, Hurricane Isaias was located over the western
Florida panhandle with maximum sustained winds of 90 mph, moving N
at 20 mph. The center of Isaias is forecast to move N to NW through
Alabama overnight and Saturday. Widespread and potentially
significant impacts to North and Central Georgia are anticipated on
the eastern side of Isaias. These include a prolonged period of
strong winds, heavy rainfall with localized flooding, and the
potential for several tornadoes. Impacts will peak in intensity
Saturday into Saturday night as Isaias moves continues into north
Alabama and into the Tennessee Valley.

The wind field associated with Isaias is expected to expand
considerably as the system moves further inland and becomes extra-
tropical. Strong winds will extend well east of the center of the
storm and into west Georgia. A Tropical Storm Warning remains in
effect for this area where wind gusts to 60 mph will be possible.
While Isaias will be weakening and becoming post-tropical, there
will be a very strong pressure gradient between the system and
strong high pressure over the Mid-Atlantic to the north and east of
the Tropical Storm Warning. This gradient will support a prolonged
period of strong easterly winds with frequent gusts to 40 to 60 mph
across most of North Georgia this afternoon into tonight. A High
Wind Warning is in effect for this area. Areas to the south and east
of these warnings have been placed in a Wind Advisory where winds
will be weaker, though gusts up to 40 mph will be possible. Across
all areas, the prolonged and strong winds could lead to power
outages from downed limbs and trees, especially when combined with
saturated soils from periods of heavy rain.

Isaias will bring widespread rainfall, with multiple bands of heavy
rain expected tonight through early Sunday. Widespread rainfall
totals of 2 to 4 inches are likely across much of the area. A
localized swath of as much as 8 inches will be possible where the
heaviest banding sets up. This rainfall could lead to flash
flooding, particularly in urban and poor-drainge areas, as well as
flood-prone creeks and streams. The north-south orientation of bands
may enhance river flooding along north south reaches. Training heavy
rain in the mountains may furthermore increase the risk of
landslides. A Flood Watch is in effect issued for the entire area,
as a result.

Additionally, as Isaias tracks northward and inland late tonight
into Saturday, a favorable environment for tornadoes will develop
first across Central Georgia, then advance into north Georgia by the
afternoon and evening. Several tornadoes will be possible,
particularly within the outer rainbands of the system. Tornadoes
from tropical systems are typically quick to develop and short-
lived, but with the forward speed of the system and the unique
setup, we can't rule out a stronger (EF2 or EF3), long-track
tornado, especially across Central Georgia.

POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* WIND:
Protect against hazardous wind having possible limited impacts across
portions of north and central Georgia. Potential impacts in this area
include:
- Damage to porches, awnings, carports, sheds, and unanchored
mobile homes. Unsecured lightweight objects blown about.
- Many large tree limbs broken off. A few trees snapped or
uprooted, but with greater numbers in places where trees are
shallow rooted. Some fences and roadway signs blown over.
- A few roads impassable from debris, particularly within urban
or heavily wooded places. Hazardous driving conditions on
bridges and other elevated roadways.
- Scattered power and communications outages.


* FLOODING RAIN:
Protect against life-threatening rainfall flooding having possible
extensive impacts across north and central Georgia. Potential impacts
include:
- Major rainfall flooding may prompt many evacuations and rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may rapidly overflow their banks in
multiple places. Small streams, creeks, canals, arroyos, and
ditches may become dangerous rivers. In mountain areas,
destructive runoff may run quickly down valleys while
increasing susceptibility to rockslides and mudslides. Flood
control systems and barriers may become stressed.
- Flood waters can enter many structures within multiple
communities, some structures becoming uninhabitable or washed
away. Many places where flood waters may cover escape routes.
Streets and parking lots become rivers of moving water with
underpasses submerged. Driving conditions become dangerous.
Many road and bridge closures with some weakened or washed out.


* TORNADOES:
Protect against a dangerous tornado event having possible significant
impacts across north and central Georgia. Potential impacts include:
- The occurrence of scattered tornadoes can hinder the execution
of emergency plans during tropical events.
- Several places may experience tornado damage with a few spots
of considerable damage, power loss, and communications failures.
- Locations could realize roofs torn off frame houses, mobile homes
demolished, boxcars overturned, large trees snapped or uprooted,
vehicles tumbled, and small boats tossed about. Dangerous
projectiles can add to the toll.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials.

* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:
Now is the time to complete all preparations to protect life and
property in accordance with your emergency plan. Ensure you are in a
safe location before the onset of strong winds or possible flooding.

Keep cell phones well charged. Cell phone chargers for automobiles
can be helpful, but be aware of your risk for deadly carbon monoxide
poisoning if your car is left idling in a garage or other poorly
ventilated area.

It is important to remain calm, informed, and focused during an
emergency. Be patient and helpful with those you encounter.

If you are a visitor, be sure to know the name of the city or town in
which you are staying and the name of the county or parish in which
it resides. Listen for these locations in local news updates. Pay
attention for instructions from local authorities.

Rapidly rising flood waters are deadly. If you are in a flood-prone
area, consider moving to higher ground. Never drive through a flooded
roadway. Remember, turn around don't drown!

If a Tornado Warning is issued for your area, be ready to shelter
quickly, preferably away from windows and in an interior room not
prone to flooding. If driving, scan the roadside for quick shelter
options.

If in a place that is vulnerable to high wind, such as near large
trees, a manufactured home, upper floors of a high-rise building, or
on a boat, consider moving to a safer shelter before the onset of
strong winds or flooding.

Closely monitor weather.gov, NOAA Weather radio or local news outlets
for official storm information. Be ready to adapt to possible changes
to the forecast. Ensure you have multiple ways to receive weather
warnings.

- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov

-----------

Service in Peachtree City GA around 5 AM, or sooner if conditions
warrant.

properties.headline: Tropical Storm Watch issued October 9 at 8:23PM PDT by NWS San Diego CA
properties.description:
* LOCATIONS AFFECTED
- Oceanside
- Carlsbad
- Chula Vista
- San Diego

* WIND
- LATEST LOCAL FORECAST: Below tropical storm force wind
- Peak Wind Forecast: 10-20 mph with gusts to 30 mph

- THREAT TO LIFE AND PROPERTY THAT INCLUDES TYPICAL FORECAST
UNCERTAINTY IN TRACK, SIZE AND INTENSITY: Potential for wind 39
to 57 mph
- The wind threat has remained nearly steady from the
previous assessment.
- PLAN: Plan for hazardous wind of equivalent tropical storm
force.
- PREPARE: Efforts to protect property should now be
underway. Prepare for limited wind damage.
- ACT: Act now to complete preparations before the wind
becomes hazardous.

- POTENTIAL IMPACTS: Limited
- Damage to porches, awnings, carports, sheds, and unanchored
mobile homes. Unsecured lightweight objects blown about.
- Many large tree limbs broken off. A few trees snapped or
uprooted, but with greater numbers in places where trees
are shallow rooted, especially in coastal and valley
locations that don't typically experience strong winds.
Some fences and roadway signs blown over.
- A few roads impassable from debris, particularly within
urban or heavily wooded places. Hazardous driving
conditions on bridges and other elevated roadways.
- Scattered power and communications outages.

* STORM SURGE
- While true storm surge is unlikely, significant coastal flooding
and beach erosion from tides over 7 feet, high surf, and
increased onshore winds expected.

- THREAT TO LIFE AND PROPERTY THAT INCLUDES TYPICAL FORECAST
UNCERTAINTY IN TRACK, SIZE AND INTENSITY: Little to no storm
surge flooding
- The storm surge threat has remained nearly steady from the
previous assessment.
- PLAN: Coastal flooding, rough surf, coastal erosion, and
life-threatening rip currents are possible.
- PREPARE: Do not make plans to go to the beach. Take necessary
actions to protect flood prone property.
- ACT: Follow the instructions of local officials. Monitor
forecasts.

- POTENTIAL IMPACTS: Significant coastal flooding and beach erosion
possible. Dangerous swimming conditions due to high surf and
strong rip currents.

* FLOODING RAIN
- LATEST LOCAL FORECAST: Flood Watch is in effect
- Peak Rainfall Amounts: Around 1 inch

- THREAT TO LIFE AND PROPERTY THAT INCLUDES TYPICAL FORECAST
UNCERTAINTY IN TRACK, SIZE AND INTENSITY: Potential for major
flooding rain
- The flooding rain threat has remained nearly steady from
the previous assessment.
- PLAN: Emergency plans should include the potential for
major flooding from heavy rain. Evacuations and rescues are
likely.
- PREPARE: Strongly consider protective actions, especially
if you are in an area vulnerable to flooding.
- ACT: Heed any flood watches and warnings. Failure to take
action will likely result in serious injury or loss of life.

- POTENTIAL IMPACTS: Extensive
- Major rainfall flooding may prompt many evacuations and
rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may rapidly overflow their banks in
multiple places. Small streams, creeks, canals, arroyos,
and ditches may become dangerous rivers. In mountain areas,
destructive runoff may run quickly down valleys while
increasing susceptibility to rockslides and mudslides.
Flood control systems and barriers may become stressed.
- Flood waters can enter many structures within multiple
communities, some structures becoming uninhabitable or
washed away. Many places where flood waters may cover
escape routes. Streets and parking lots become rivers of
moving water with underpasses submerged. Driving conditions
become dangerous. Many road and bridge closures with some
weakened or washed out.

* TORNADO
- LATEST LOCAL FORECAST:
- Situation is unfavorable for tornadoes

- THREAT TO LIFE AND PROPERTY THAT INCLUDES TYPICAL FORECAST
UNCERTAINTY IN TRACK, SIZE AND INTENSITY: Tornadoes not expected
- The tornado threat has remained nearly steady from the
previous assessment.
- PLAN: Tornadoes are not expected. Showers and thunderstorms
with gusty winds may still occur.
- PREPARE: Little to no preparations needed to protect
against tornadoes at this time. Keep informed of the latest
tornado situation.
- ACT: Listen for changes in the forecast.

- POTENTIAL IMPACTS: Little to None
- Little to no potential impacts from tornadoes.

* FOR MORE INFORMATION:
- sdcountyemergency.com

properties.headline: Tropical Cyclone Local Statement issued October 9 at 11:22PM EDT by NWS Tallahassee FL
properties.description:
HLSTAE

This product covers eastern Florida panhandle, Florida Big Bend, southeastern Alabama and southwestern Georgia

**ISAIAS MOVING INLAND OVER THE WESTERN FLORIDA PANHANDLE**

NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- None

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- A Storm Surge Warning and Hurricane Warning are in effect for
Coastal Bay and South Walton
- A Hurricane Warning is in effect for Central Walton, Coffee,
Geneva, Holmes, Inland Bay, North Walton, and Washington
- A Storm Surge Warning and Tropical Storm Warning are in effect
for Coastal Franklin, Coastal Gulf, Coastal Jefferson, and
Coastal Wakulla
- A Storm Surge Warning is in effect for Coastal Dixie and
Coastal Taylor
- A Tropical Storm Warning is in effect for Baker, Calhoun,
Calhoun, Clay, Colquitt, Dale, Decatur, Dougherty, Early,
Gadsden, Grady, Henry, Houston, Inland Franklin, Inland Gulf,
Inland Jefferson, Inland Wakulla, Jackson, Lee, Leon, Miller,
Mitchell, Northern Liberty, Quitman, Randolph, Seminole,
Southern Liberty, Terrell, Thomas, and Worth

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 70 miles northwest of Panama City or about 120 miles
northwest of Apalachicola
- 30.8N 86.5W
- Storm Intensity 90 mph
- Movement North or 5 degrees at 20 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

...DAMAGING WIND GUSTS...FLOODING RAINS...AND A FEW TORNADOES
POSSIBLE THROUGH THE OVERNIGHT HOURS INTO SATURDAY...

At 11 PM ET, Hurricane Isaias was located over the western Florida
Panhandle with winds of 90 mph and moving N at 20 mph. Isaias is
forecast to continue on a northward track through the overnight
hours and move into Alabama. Now inland, the peak winds of the
hurricane will gradually weaken. However, a considerably large wind
field combined with displaced convection east of the track will
continue to generate impacts well beyond the forecast cone,
particularly east of the hurricane's center.

Conditions will remain dangerous across the Florida Panhandle and
Big Bend, Southeast Alabama, and Southwest Georgia for the next
several hours. Residents should remain in a safe location until
conditions improve.

A Storm Surge Warning remains in effect for the all of our Panhandle
and Big Bend coast. Life-threatening inundation values of 3 to 5
feet above normally dry ground remain possible along the Panhandle
coast east to the Aucilla River and 2 to 4 feet from the Aucilla
River to the Suwannee River. Coastal saltwater flooding may linger
through Saturday from persistent onshore flow.

Soggy conditions across the region from recent rainfall will make
much of the Tri-state area more sensitive to flooding from
additional heavy rainfall from Isaias. Forecast rainfall totals of 4
to 8 inches are expected across much of the area from the storm.
Localized totals up to 15 inches are possible, especially within
banding across the Florida Panhandle and Big Bend. Such values would
be capable of producing isolated to scattered flash flooding.
Localized considerable flash flooding is also possible where bands
of heavy rain move repeatedly over the same area. Given these
factors, a Flood Watch is in effect for the Tri-State area through
Saturday evening. Minor to isolated moderate river flooding appears
likely from the anticipated rain.

Isaias will also bring a heightened tornado risk across the Florida
Panhandle and FL Big Bend overnight into Saturday and Southeast AL &
Southwest GA late tonight into Saturday.

POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* WIND:
Potential impacts from the main wind event are now unfolding across
the Tri-State area. Remain well sheltered from life-threatening wind
having devastating impacts. If realized, these impacts include:
- Structural damage to sturdy buildings, some with complete roof
and wall failures. Complete destruction of mobile homes. Damage
greatly accentuated by large airborne projectiles. Locations
may be uninhabitable for weeks or months.
- Numerous large trees snapped or uprooted along with fences and
roadway signs blown over.
- Many roads impassable from large debris, and more within urban
or heavily wooded places. Many bridges, causeways, and access
routes impassable.
- Widespread power and communications outages.

Potential impacts from the main wind event are expected to continue
across the Tri-State area. Remain well sheltered from life-
threatening wind having limited to extensive impacts.

* SURGE:
Potential impacts from the main surge event are now unfolding across
the Florida Panhandle and western Big Bend coast. Remain well away
from life-threatening surge having possible significant impacts. If
realized, these impacts include:
- Areas of inundation with storm surge flooding accentuated by
waves. Damage to several buildings, mainly near the coast.
- Sections of near-shore escape routes and secondary roads become
weakened or washed out, especially in usually vulnerable low
spots.
- Major beach erosion with heavy surf breaching dunes. Strong and
numerous rip currents.
- Moderate damage to marinas, docks, boardwalks, and piers.
Several small craft broken away from moorings, especially in
unprotected anchorages.

Elsewhere across eastern Florida panhandle, Florida Big Bend,
southeastern Alabama and southwestern Georgia, little to no impact is
anticipated.

* FLOODING RAIN:
Potential impacts from the flooding rain are still unfolding across
much of the Florida Panhandle, Big Bend and Southeast Alabama into
Southwest Georgia. Remain well guarded against life-threatening flood
waters having possible devastating impacts. If realized, these impacts
include:
- Extreme rainfall flooding may prompt numerous evacuations and
rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may overwhelmingly overflow their banks
in many places with deep moving water. Small streams, creeks,
and ditches may become raging rivers. Flood control systems and
barriers may become stressed.
- Flood waters can enter numerous structures within multiple
communities, some structures becoming uninhabitable or washed
away. Numerous places where flood waters may cover escape
routes. Streets and parking lots become rivers of raging water
with underpasses submerged. Driving conditions become very
dangerous. Numerous road and bridge closures with some weakened
or washed out.

* TORNADOES:
Potential impacts from tornadoes are still unfolding across the eastern
Florida Panhandle, Florida Big Bend, into Southeast Alabama and Southwest
Georgia. Remain well braced against a dangerous tornado
event having possible significant impacts. If
realized, these impacts include:
- The occurrence of scattered tornadoes can hinder the execution
of emergency plans during tropical events.
- Several places may experience tornado damage with a few spots
of considerable damage, power loss, and communications failures.
- Locations could realize roofs torn off frame houses, mobile
homes demolished, boxcars overturned, large trees snapped or
uprooted, vehicles tumbled, and small boats tossed about.
Dangerous projectiles can add to the toll.



PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials.

* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:
Now is the time to stay inside and away from windows. Listen for
updates and be ready in case you lose electrical power. Keep a
battery- powered radio, charged cell phone and flashlight handy.

During the peak of the storm be ready to move quickly. Keep your
shoes on and rain gear handy. Boots and athletic shoes offer the best
foot protection if you become unexpectedly exposed to the weather.

Keep your cell phone charged and in power-saving mode. If you lose
power, use it sparingly and mainly for personal emergencies and
check-ins.

If a tornado warning is issued for your area, quickly move to the
safest place within your shelter. Protect your head and body.

* ADDITIONAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION:
- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

NEXT UPDATE
-----------

The next local statement will be issued by the National Weather
Service in Tallahassee FL around 530 AM EDT, or sooner if conditions
warrant.

properties.description:
HLSLIX

This product covers Southeast Louisiana and South Mississippi

**ISAIAS MOVING INLAND INTO SOUTH CENTRAL ALABAMA**

NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- All watches and warnings have been canceled

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- None

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 230 miles east-northeast of New Orleans LA or about 150
miles east of Gulfport MS
- 30.8N 86.5W
- Storm Intensity 90 mph
- Movement North or 5 degrees at 20 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

Hurricane Isaias has made landfall over the northwest Florida
panhandle as a dangerous category 2 hurricane this evening. Hurricane
Isaias will continue to move inland and rapidly weaken overnight
tonight and Saturday morning. Winds have started to decrease across
our region as the storm continues downstream. Because of this we have
cancelled all Hurricane and Tropical Storm Watches and warnings. There
could still be some minor coastal flooding up to 3 feet, especially
along the Mississippi Gulf Coast. The Storm Surge Warning has been
replaced with a Coastal Flood Advisory through the next tide cycle
early Saturday morning.

POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* WIND:
Little to no additional impacts are anticipated at this time
across Southeast Louisiana and South Mississippi.

* SURGE:
Minor to no additional surge impacts expected.

- Community officials are now assessing the extent of actual
surge impacts accordingly.


Elsewhere across Southeast Louisiana and South Mississippi, little to
no impact is anticipated.

* FLOODING RAIN:
No additional impacts are anticipated at this time
across Southeast Louisiana and South Mississippi.

* TORNADOES:
No additional impacts are anticipated at this time
across Southeast Louisiana and South Mississippi.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials.


* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:

Check in with your emergency points of contact. Let them know your
location and status. Keep conversations short and to the point. Do
not tie up communications systems.

Check on your neighbors. If necessary, help them connect with their
points of contact.

Do not go sightseeing within impacted communities. Sightseers
interfere with the emergency work of first responders.

When inspecting damage, use flashlights rather than candles or flamed
lanterns. Be aware of sparks that can ignite natural gas or other
leaking flammables.

Do not go up on your roof until the weather conditions are safe.
Ladders can be slippery in the rain and unexpected wind gusts can
blow you off the roof.

When clearing out fallen trees, be careful with chainsaws and axes.
Always wear protective gear and keep others at a safe distance.
Leaning trees and those which have fallen on roofs or power lines can
be especially dangerous. If you are not in good health or unsure
about what you are doing, have someone with tree cutting experience
do the job. Never cut trees without a partner.

If using a generator, avoid carbon monoxide poisoning by following
instructions provided by the manufacturer. Operate your generator in
a well-ventilated space outside of your living area and away from
open doors and windows.


* ADDITIONAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION:
- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov
- For information on creating an emergency plan see getagameplan.org
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

NEXT UPDATE
-----------

As it pertains to this event...this will be the last local statement
issued by the National Weather Service in New Orleans LA regarding
the effects of Hurricane Isaias.

properties.headline: Tropical Cyclone Local Statement issued October 9 at 10:09PM CDT by NWS Birmingham AL
properties.description:
HLSBMX

This product covers Central Alabama

**Isaias continues to move north across Alabama this evening**

NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- None

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- A Tropical Storm Warning is in effect for Autauga, Barbour,
Bibb, Bullock, Chambers, Chilton, Clay, Coosa, Dallas, Elmore,
Fayette, Greene, Hale, Jefferson, Lamar, Lee, Lowndes, Macon,
Marengo, Marion, Montgomery, Perry, Pickens, Pike, Randolph,
Russell, Shelby, St. Clair, Sumter, Talladega, Tallapoosa,
Tuscaloosa, Walker, and Winston

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 190 miles south of Birmingham AL or about 110 miles south
of Montgomery AL
- 30.8N 86.5W
- Storm Intensity 90 mph
- Movement North or 5 degrees at 20 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

Hurricane Isaias made landfall earlier this evening near Destin, FL
with max sustained winds of 105 MPH and a central pressure of 971 mb.
The system will gradually weaken as it continues to move north across
the state. As it weakens, the wind field will expand, overspreading
most of Central Alabama. Winds will gust as high as 50 to 60+ mph late
tonight through Saturday, resulting in the potential for widespread
downed trees and power lines. Rainfall amounts of 1.5 to 4 inches with
locally higher amounts up to 5 inches will result in the potential for
flash flooding, especially in urban and other poor drainage areas.
Isolated tornadoes may develop across far southeast portions of Central
Alabama.

POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* WIND:
Potential impacts from the main wind event are now unfolding across
southern portions of Central Alabama. Remain well sheltered from
dangerous wind having significant impacts. If realized, these impacts
include:
- Some damage to roofing and siding materials, along with damage
to porches, awnings, carports, and sheds. A few buildings
experiencing window, door, and garage door failures. Mobile and
manufactured homes damaged, especially if unanchored. Unsecured
lightweight objects become dangerous projectiles.
- Several large trees snapped or uprooted. Several fences and
roadway signs blown over.
- Some roads impassable from large debris, and more within urban
or heavily wooded places.
- Scattered power and communications outages, but more prevalent
in areas with above ground lines.

Potential impacts from the main wind event will spread north across
Central Alabama. Remain well sheltered from hazardous wind.

* FLOODING RAIN:
Potential impacts from the flooding rain are still unfolding across
southern portions of Central Alabama. Remain well guarded against
life- threatening flood waters having extensive impacts. If realized,
these impacts include:
- Major rainfall flooding may prompt many evacuations and rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may rapidly overflow their banks in
multiple places. Small streams, creeks, and ditches may become
dangerous rivers. Flood control systems and barriers may become
stressed.
- Flood waters can enter many structures within multiple
communities, some structures becoming uninhabitable or washed
away. Streets and parking lots become rivers of moving water
with underpasses submerged. Driving conditions become
dangerous. Many road and bridge closures with some weakened or
washed out.

Potential impacts from the flooding rain will spread north across
Central Alabama. Remain well guarded against dangerous flood waters
having additional significant impacts.

* TORNADOES:
Potential impacts from tornadoes are still unfolding across southeast
Central Alabama. Remain well braced against a tornado event having
possible limited impacts. If realized, these impacts include:
- A few places may experience tornado damage, along with power
and communications disruptions.
- Locations could realize roofs peeled off buildings, chimneys
toppled, mobile and manufactured homes pushed off foundations
or overturned, downed trees, and moving vehicles blown off
roads.

Elsewhere across Central Alabama, little to no impact is anticipated.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials.

* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:
Now is the time to stay inside and away from windows. Listen for
updates and be ready in case you lose electrical power. Keep a battery-
powered radio, charged cell phone and flashlight handy.

Keep your cell phone charged and in power-saving mode. If you lose
power, use it sparingly and mainly for personal emergencies and
check-ins.

Do not be a thrill seeker or risk your life for senseless photos or
videos.

Quickly move to the safest place within your shelter if it begins to
fail, preferably an interior room on the lowest floor as long as
flooding is not a concern.

If a tornado warning is issued for your area, quickly move to the
safest place within your shelter. Protect your head and body.


* ADDITIONAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION:
- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov
- For information on creating an emergency plan see getagameplan.org
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

NEXT UPDATE
-----------

The next local statement will be issued by the National Weather
Service in Birmingham AL around 4 AM CDT, or sooner if conditions
warrant.

rain across the warned area. Flash flooding is ongoing or expected to
begin shortly.

flash flooding.

SOURCE...Radar indicated.

areas, highways, streets and underpasses.

Geneva, Samson, Kinston, Coffee Springs, Sellersville, Spears,
Marl, Lytle, Logan Field Municipal A/P, Marvin Chapel, Pera, Ganer,
Chancellor, Weeks, Lucile, Earlytown, Vaughanville, Holley Store,
Somerset and Geneva Municipal A/P.

Isaias has fallen over the warned area, which has likely exacerbated
flooding conditions.
properties.instruction:

deaths occur in vehicles.

Move to higher ground now. Act quickly to protect your life.

Be especially cautious at night when it is harder to recognize the
dangers of flooding.

properties.areaDesc: Inland Bay
properties.headline: Hurricane Warning issued October 9 at 10:57PM EDT by NWS Tallahassee FL
properties.description:
* LOCATIONS AFFECTED
- Youngstown
- Fountain

* WIND
- LATEST LOCAL FORECAST: Below tropical storm force wind
- Peak Wind Forecast: 25-35 mph with gusts to 60 mph

- THREAT TO LIFE AND PROPERTY THAT INCLUDES TYPICAL FORECAST
UNCERTAINTY IN TRACK, SIZE AND INTENSITY: Potential for wind 58
to 73 mph
- The wind threat has remained nearly steady from the
previous assessment.
- PLAN: Plan for dangerous wind of equivalent strong tropical
storm force.
- PREPARE: Remaining efforts to protect life and property
should be completed as soon as possible. Prepare for
significant wind damage.
- ACT: Move to safe shelter before the wind becomes hazardous.

- POTENTIAL IMPACTS: Significant
- Some damage to roofing and siding materials, along with
damage to porches, awnings, carports, and sheds. A few
buildings experiencing window, door, and garage door
failures. Mobile homes damaged, especially if unanchored.
Unsecured lightweight objects become dangerous projectiles.
- Several large trees snapped or uprooted, but with greater
numbers in places where trees are shallow rooted. Several
fences and roadway signs blown over.
- Some roads impassable from large debris, and more within
urban or heavily wooded places. A few bridges, causeways,
and access routes impassable.
- Scattered power and communications outages, but more
prevalent in areas with above ground lines.

* STORM SURGE
- No storm surge inundation forecast

- THREAT TO LIFE AND PROPERTY THAT INCLUDES TYPICAL FORECAST
UNCERTAINTY IN TRACK, SIZE AND INTENSITY: Little to no storm
surge flooding
- The storm surge threat has remained nearly steady from the
previous assessment.
- PLAN: There is little to no threat of storm surge flooding.
Rough surf, coastal erosion, and life-threatening rip
currents are possible.
- PREPARE: Little to no preparations for storm surge flooding
are needed.
- ACT: Follow the instructions of local officials. Monitor
forecasts.

- POTENTIAL IMPACTS: Little to None
- Little to no potential impacts from storm surge flooding.

* FLOODING RAIN
- LATEST LOCAL FORECAST: Flood Watch is in effect
- Peak Rainfall Amounts: No additional significant rainfall
forecast

- THREAT TO LIFE AND PROPERTY THAT INCLUDES TYPICAL FORECAST
UNCERTAINTY IN TRACK, SIZE AND INTENSITY: Potential for major
flooding rain
- The flooding rain threat has remained nearly steady from
the previous assessment.
- PLAN: Emergency plans should include the potential for
major flooding from heavy rain. Evacuations and rescues are
likely.
- PREPARE: Strongly consider protective actions, especially
if you are in an area vulnerable to flooding.
- ACT: Heed any flood watches and warnings. Failure to take
action will likely result in serious injury or loss of life.

- POTENTIAL IMPACTS: Extensive
- Major rainfall flooding may prompt many evacuations and
rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may rapidly overflow their banks in
multiple places. Small streams, creeks, and ditches may
become dangerous rivers. Flood control systems and barriers
may become stressed.
- Flood waters can enter many structures within multiple
communities, some structures becoming uninhabitable or
washed away. Many places where flood waters may cover
escape routes. Streets and parking lots become rivers of
moving water with underpasses submerged. Driving conditions
become dangerous. Many road and bridge closures with some
weakened or washed out.

* TORNADO
- LATEST LOCAL FORECAST:
- Situation is favorable for tornadoes

- THREAT TO LIFE AND PROPERTY THAT INCLUDES TYPICAL FORECAST
UNCERTAINTY IN TRACK, SIZE AND INTENSITY: Potential for several
tornadoes
- The tornado threat has decreased from the previous
assessment.
- PLAN: Emergency plans should include the potential for
several tornadoes with a few possibly intense having larger
damage paths.
- PREPARE: Those living in manufactured homes or on boats are
urged to relocate to safe shelter before hazardous weather
arrives.
- ACT: Listen for tornado watches and warnings. If a tornado
warning is issued, be ready to shelter quickly.

- POTENTIAL IMPACTS: Significant
- The occurrence of scattered tornadoes can hinder the
execution of emergency plans during tropical events.
- Several places may experience tornado damage with a few
spots of considerable damage, power loss, and
communications failures.
- Locations could realize roofs torn off frame houses, mobile
homes demolished, boxcars overturned, large trees snapped
or uprooted, vehicles tumbled, and small boats tossed
about. Dangerous projectiles can add to the toll.

* FOR MORE INFORMATION:
- Local Weather Conditions and Forecasts: NWS Tallahassee
- https://www.weather.gov/tallahassee
- Information from the Florida Division of Emergency Management
- https://www.floridadisaster.org
- Information from Bay County Emergency Management
- http://www.baycountyfl.gov/EmergencyManagement

properties.areaDesc: Rabun; Habersham; Stephens; Franklin; Hart; Elbert; Avery; Yancey; Mitchell; Haywood; Buncombe; Northern Jackson; Macon; Southern Jackson; Transylvania; Henderson; Caldwell Mountains; Greater Caldwell; Burke Mountains; Greater Burke; McDowell Mountains; Eastern McDowell; Rutherford Mountains; Greater Rutherford; Polk Mountains; Eastern Polk; Oconee Mountains; Pickens Mountains; Greenville Mountains; Greater Oconee
properties.headline: Flood Watch issued October 9 at 10:48PM EDT until October 11 at 2:00PM EDT by NWS Greenville-Spartanburg SC
properties.description:
* WHAT...Flash flooding caused by excessive rainfall continues to be
possible.

* WHERE...Portions of northeast Georgia, including the following
counties, Elbert, Franklin, Habersham, Hart, Rabun and Stephens;
portions of western North Carolina, including the following
counties, Avery, Buncombe, Burke, Caldwell, Haywood, Henderson,
Jackson, Macon, McDowell, Mitchell, Polk, Rutherford, Transylvania
and Yancey; portions of Upstate South Carolina, including Oconee
County, and mountainous northern portions of Pickens and Greenville
Counties.

* WHEN...From 8 AM EDT Saturday through Sunday afternoon.

* IMPACTS...Excessive runoff may result in flooding of rivers,
creeks, streams, and other low-lying and flood-prone locations.
Creeks and streams may rise out of their banks. Low-water crossings
may be flooded.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...
- As Isaias weakens and moves northward through the Mid-South early
Saturday, rain will become increasingly likely across the western
Carolinas and northeast Georgia. Periods of rain may begin over
the watch area prior to dawn Saturday, though rainfall rates will
initially be light. Rainfall rates will increase during the day,
and heavy rain is most likely Saturday afternoon through early
Sunday morning, particularly along the south and east facing Blue
Ridge Escarpment, that is, near the southern border of North
Carolina west of I-26, and in the sharp terrain from near Saluda
to Grandfather Mountain in North Carolina.
- http://www.weather.gov/safety/flood
properties.instruction:
A Flood Watch for flash flooding means there is a potential for rapid
onset flooding based on current forecasts. Flash flooding is a very
dangerous situation and may impact areas that do not typically flood.
Please monitor the latest forecasts and be prepared to take action
quickly should Flash Flood Warnings be issued.

Rainfall of more than five inches in similar storms has been
associated with an increased risk of landslides, especially
fast-moving debris flows and debris slides. If you live on a
mountainside or in a cove at the base of a mountain, especially near
a stream, be ready to leave in advance of the storm and follow
evacuation orders from local officials. Consider postponing travel
along mountain roads during the heavy rainfall event.

properties.areaDesc: Dale, AL; Geneva, AL; Henry, AL; Houston, AL
properties.headline: Flash Flood Warning issued October 9 at 10:31PM EDT until October 10 at 4:30AM EDT by NWS Tallahassee FL
properties.description:
FFWTAE

The National Weather Service in Tallahassee has issued a

* Flash Flood Warning for...
Dale County in southeastern Alabama...
Eastern Geneva County in southeastern Alabama...
Southwestern Henry County in southeastern Alabama...
Houston County in southeastern Alabama...

* Until 330 AM CDT.

* At 931 PM CDT, Doppler radar indicated thunderstorms producing
heavy rain across the warned area. Flash flooding is ongoing or
expected to begin shortly.

HAZARD...Flash flooding caused by thunderstorms.

SOURCE...Radar indicated.

IMPACT...Flash flooding of small creeks and streams, urban areas,
highways, streets and underpasses as well as other poor
drainage and low-lying areas.

* Some locations that will experience flash flooding include...
Daleville, Cottonwood, Dothan, Headland, Ozark, Fort Rucker,
Enterprise, Hartford, Taylor, Midland City, Kinsey, Ashford, Level
Plains, Slocomb, Cowarts, Newton, Webb, Ariton and Pinckard.

An extensive outer rainband from Isaias will produce heavy rainfall
capable of flash flooding as embedded cells move southeast to
northwest repeatedly over the same locations within the warned area.
properties.instruction:
Turn around, don't drown when encountering flooded roads. Most flood
deaths occur in vehicles.

Be especially cautious at night when it is harder to recognize the
dangers of flooding.

Be aware of your surroundings and do not drive on flooded roads.

properties.headline: Special Weather Statement issued October 9 at 8:52PM EDT by NWS Jackson KY
properties.description:
A period of strong wind gusts is expected on Saturday as the
remnants of Hurricane Isaias move into eastern Kentucky.
Southeasterly winds of 10 to 20 mph, with gusts up to 35 mph are
expected. The strongest winds are expected during the afternoon
and should coincide with the arrival of the leading bands of rain.
Once rainfall becomes steady, many areas will see the winds
lighten, except at elevations above 1,500 feet, where the gusty
winds are expected to continue into Saturday night. Isolated gusts
over 40 mph are possible over the highest ridge tops. The gusty
winds could blow around unsecured outdoor objects and decor.

properties.description:
* WHAT...Dangerous rip currents and strong longshore currents in
the surf zone.

* WHERE...Crystal Coast beaches.

* WHEN...From 8 AM EDT Saturday through Saturday evening.

* IMPACTS...Rip currents can sweep even the best swimmers away
from shore into deeper water. Strong longshore currents will
create dangerous swimming conditions.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...The most likely time for strong rip
currents to occur is a couple hours either side of low tide,
which will occur around 2:00 PM Saturday.
properties.instruction:
Life-threatening rip currents. If caught in a rip current, remain
calm. Swim in a direction following the shoreline. If tired,
float or tread water until out of the rip current. If unable to
escape, face the shore and call or wave for help.

Strong longshore currents can sweep swimmers and surfers into rip
currents, piers, jetties and other hazardous areas. In many
cases, the longshore current is strong enough to prevent swimmers
from being able to keep their feet on the bottom making it
difficult to return to shore.
